title: Closing the Gaps: Building One Connected Revenue Cycle
summary: A connected Revenue Cycle requires clear ownership, closed-loop handoffs, shared measures, and no unresolved account without a next action and due date.
body_markdown:
*One patient, one account, one Revenue Cycle—and no unresolved work without a clear owner.*


**By Vanessa Couch-Laguana, Head of RCM, LunaBill**


---


Healthcare organizations often describe the Revenue Cycle in terms of the front end and the back end.


The front end schedules and registers the patient, verifies coverage, secures authorizations, prepares estimates, and discusses financial responsibility. The back end submits claims, follows up with payers, manages denials, resolves balances, and communicates with patients after care.


Those distinctions may help organize departments, but they can also create silos.


A patient does not experience the Revenue Cycle as a collection of separate departments. The patient experiences one organization. Likewise, an account does not stop being connected to Patient Access when the patient leaves the registration desk. It continues through clinical care, documentation, utilization management, charge capture, coding, billing, follow-up, denial management, and patient collections.


After nearly three decades in Revenue Cycle operations, I have learned that the greatest delays often occur not within a department, but between departments—especially when work is incomplete, ownership is unclear, or one team does not know what the next team needs.


Closing those gaps requires more than stronger communication between Patient Access and Patient Financial Services. It requires the entire Revenue Cycle, including the clinical and operational departments that support it, to work as one connected system.


## The Revenue Cycle begins before the front desk


Patient Access does not begin when a patient arrives for care. It begins with scheduling, preregistration, and financial clearance.


For prescheduled services, especially surgical and procedural cases, organizations should complete as much work as possible before the patient arrives. Depending on the organization’s structure, that work may be managed by scheduling, Patient Access, a centralized preregistration team, or a dedicated financial-clearance unit.


Regardless of the department name, the responsibilities should be clear.


A complete financial-clearance process may include:


- Confirming patient demographic and insurance information
- Verifying eligibility and benefits
- Determining referral and authorization requirements
- Obtaining the required authorization
- Confirming that the scheduled service matches the authorized service
- Reviewing medical-necessity or order requirements
- Preparing an estimate of the patient’s expected responsibility
- Conducting appropriate patient outreach
- Collecting amounts due when appropriate
- Screening for financial assistance
- Screening for available coverage options, including Medicaid or Medicare when appropriate
- Escalating services that have not been financially cleared


The organization should also define exactly what “financially cleared” means. If one department considers an account cleared after eligibility is verified, while another expects authorization, an estimate, patient contact, and documentation to be completed, the account may move forward with important work still unresolved.


The[Healthcare Financial Management Association’s patient financial communication guidance](https://www.hfma.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/patient-financial-communications-best-practices-2019.pdf) recommends beginning discussions as early as possible, maintaining continuity from preregistration through the encounter, verifying insurance information, and connecting patients with estimates, payment options, or financial assistance when appropriate. That continuity can prevent patients from being asked the same questions repeatedly and can give them clearer information before care is delivered.


## Responsibility does not end when the patient leaves the desk


Registration should be completed as thoroughly as possible, but responsibility does not end when the patient is no longer standing at the registration desk.


When information remains incomplete, the account needs:


- A clearly identified owner
- A documented description of what is missing
- A required next action
- A completion timeframe
- An escalation path
- A record of previous attempts and outcomes


Without those elements, an incomplete account can become “out of sight, out of mind.” It may sit untouched until billing discovers the problem or a payer rejects or denies the claim.


By then, the organization may be trying to locate coverage information, obtain documentation, correct an authorization, or contact a patient weeks after the encounter. Staff must reconstruct what happened, patients may have difficulty remembering the details, and payer deadlines may already be approaching.


Every unresolved account should have an owner. I think of this as a no-orphan-account standard: no account should remain in the Revenue Cycle without a named owner, a next action, and a due date.


## Prescheduled and emergency services need different workflows


Organizations should not apply the same financial-clearance workflow to every patient encounter.


For prescheduled services, there is often time to verify coverage, obtain authorization, review benefits, prepare an estimate, screen for assistance, and contact the patient before the date of service. The workflow should use that time intentionally.


Emergency care is different.


Emergency care cannot always wait for financial clearance, but financial-clearance responsibility does not disappear. The organization still needs a defined process for obtaining missing information, verifying coverage, addressing authorization or notification requirements, screening for assistance, and documenting what remains unresolved.


Most importantly, those activities cannot interfere with emergency care. The Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act prohibits hospitals from delaying an appropriate medical screening examination or stabilizing treatment to ask about payment or insurance.[CMS: Know Your Rights—EMTALA](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/emtala-know-your-rights.pdf-0)


The emergency workflow should therefore define:


- What information may be collected at arrival without delaying care
- When registration and financial discussions may appropriately occur
- Who follows up when information cannot be obtained during the encounter
- Who submits required admission notifications
- Who reviews failed or rejected notifications
- How unresolved coverage and authorization issues are escalated
- How patients are connected with financial assistance after stabilization or discharge


The objective is not to abandon the financial process. It is to complete it at the appropriate time without placing care at risk.


## Standardize the work for unresolved accounts


When staff cannot obtain required information, the next step should not depend entirely on individual judgment.


Organizations should establish a standard unresolved-account process that defines:


- How many outreach attempts are required
- When those attempts should occur
- Which communication methods may be used
- What information employees should request
- What information should be provided to the patient
- Where attempts and outcomes must be documented
- When the account should be escalated
- Who receives the escalation
- How quickly the receiving person must respond
- When financial-assistance or coverage screening should begin


Patient conversations should also be supported by consistent, patient-friendly scripts. Employees need language that explains why information is being requested, what the patient may owe, where the estimate came from, and what assistance may be available.


For tax-exempt hospital facilities, federal requirements under Section 501(r) include maintaining and publicizing a written financial-assistance policy that explains eligibility and how patients may apply. The requirements also reinforce that financial-assistance processes must be implemented consistently, not simply documented in a policy.[IRS: Financial Assistance and Emergency Medical Care Policies under Section 501(r)(4)](https://www.irs.gov/charities-non-profits/financial-assistance-policy-and-emergency-medical-care-policy-section-501r4)


Financial assistance should not be treated as the last option after repeated collection attempts. When a patient may qualify, screening should begin as early as practical.


## Moving an account is not the same as completing a handoff


An account can be moved from one workqueue to another without responsibility truly being transferred.


A complete handoff should tell the receiving department:


- What has already been completed
- What remains unresolved
- What attempts have been made
- What supporting documentation is available
- What deadline or financial risk applies
- What action is expected next
- Who previously owned the work
- Who owns it now
- When further escalation is required


The receiving department must also have the access, information, capacity, and authority needed to act.


Ownership should remain with the sending department until the receiving department has the information, access, and authority needed to accept responsibility for the next action.


This is what makes the handoff closed-loop. The work is not considered transferred merely because someone routed the account. The receiving team must be able to see the history, understand the outstanding issue, and accept responsibility for the next action.


Leaders should apply this principle throughout the Revenue Cycle, not only between Patient Access and Patient Financial Services.


## Clinical documentation, coding, and charge capture are part of the same cycle


An account may be fully registered and financially cleared but still remain unbillable.


Clinical documentation may be incomplete. An order may not support the service performed. A coding query may be awaiting a response. Charges may be missing. The documented level of care may not align with the claim. A medical-necessity concern may remain unresolved.


These are not separate clinical or coding problems. They are Revenue Cycle issues with clinical, compliance, financial, and patient consequences.


CMS notes that incomplete or insufficient medical records can result in payment denials when the documentation does not support the services performed, medical necessity, or the level of care billed.[CMS: Complying with Medical Record Documentation Requirements](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/certmedrecdoc10workgroup.pdf)


That is why a complete Revenue Cycle review should include:


- Clinical documentation completion
- Unsigned or incomplete orders
- Medical-necessity issues
- Utilization-management delays
- Coding backlogs
- Unanswered coding or clinical-documentation queries
- Charge-capture delays
- Late or missing charges
- Claims held for documentation or coding
- Services that do not match the authorization
- Accounts that cannot meet the organization’s “ready to bill” definition


Just as “financially cleared” should have a consistent definition, “ready to bill” should mean the same thing to clinical departments, coding, billing, and leadership.


## Feedback should lead to correction


Patient Financial Services should provide account-specific feedback when a correction is needed. It should also identify recurring trends that may indicate a larger problem.


However, sending the same report every month is not improvement.


Feedback should result in an action plan when the data shows a pattern. That action plan should identify:


- The issue and its financial or operational impact
- The root cause
- The department or role responsible for correction
- The actions that will be taken
- The accountable owner
- The completion deadline
- The measure that will show whether the correction worked
- The escalation path if the action is not completed


An action plan should not be closed simply because training occurred or a meeting was held. It should close only after the related KPI, aging, accuracy, or denial trend demonstrates sustained improvement.


Organizations should not wait until the next monthly meeting to address a high-risk account, a high-dollar claim, or an issue approaching a timely-filing deadline. Account-specific feedback must occur quickly enough for the organization to protect its ability to bill and collect.


A practical review cadence may include:


- Immediate escalation for high-risk, high-dollar, patient-sensitive, or deadline-driven accounts
- Biweekly cross-functional review of recurring trends, stalled accounts, missed handoffs, and departments not meeting key performance indicators
- Monthly senior-leadership reporting on performance, root causes, unresolved barriers, corrective actions, and accountability


Senior leaders should receive at least a monthly report so they understand what is being discussed, where accounts are repeatedly becoming stalled, which performance gaps are continuing, and whether action plans are progressing.


Every senior-leadership report should answer six questions: Where is work becoming stalled? How many accounts and dollars are affected? What is the effect on patients or care delivery? What is the root cause? Who owns the corrective action? By what date should improvement be visible?


The process owner or designated operational leader should be responsible for identifying the owner of each corrective action, confirming that the person has the authority and resources to act, and documenting the due date and expected result. Reporting becomes valuable when it leads to a decision, an accountable next step, and confirmation that the correction produced a measurable result.


## Review the entire Revenue Cycle scorecard


A cross-functional review should not focus only on front-end errors or back-end results.


It should include representatives from the functions affecting the account, such as:


- Scheduling and preregistration
- Registration
- Eligibility and financial clearance
- Authorization and utilization management
- Clinical operations
- Clinical documentation improvement
- Coding
- Charge capture
- Billing and claims
- Insurance follow-up
- Denial and appeal management
- Patient Financial Services
- Financial counseling and assistance
- Information technology
- Managed care or payer relations, when appropriate


The team should review each area’s KPIs and goals, but it should also examine how performance in one area affects the next.


The scorecard should distinguish leading indicators from lagging outcomes. Preregistration completion, authorization turnaround, documentation timeliness, coding-query aging, and charge lag can reveal a problem before it becomes a denial or aged receivable. Denials, cash, write-offs, and patient complaints show the eventual result. Leaders need both views to intervene early and confirm whether the intervention worked.


A useful monthly report may include:


- Preregistration completion
- Financial-clearance completion
- Eligibility and authorization denials
- Authorization turnaround time
- Point-of-service collections
- Estimates completed before service
- Financial-assistance screening
- Missing or unsigned clinical documentation
- Outstanding coding and documentation queries
- Coding turnaround time and backlog
- Charge lag and late charges
- Medical-necessity and order issues
- Clean-claim rate
- Claim-edit volume and aging
- Days from service to initial bill
- Billing delays caused by missing information
- Back-end rework
- Denial volume, value, and root cause
- Appeal turnaround and success
- Accounts approaching timely-filing limits
- High-risk or high-dollar stalled accounts
- Patient billing calls and complaints
- Open and overdue corrective-action plans


These measures should not be reviewed in isolation. A department may meet its volume goal while sending incomplete work to the next team. Coding may appear current while unanswered documentation queries remain outside its queue. Registration volume may be strong while eligibility denials rise. Billing productivity may look acceptable while clinical documentation holds continue to age.


Completion volume alone does not prove that the Revenue Cycle is moving effectively.


## Measure time at every handoff


Organizations commonly measure final outcomes such as total days in accounts receivable, denial rates, or cash collections. Those measures are important, but they do not always show where the delay began.


Leaders should also measure how long accounts spend:


- Waiting for patient information
- Awaiting authorization
- Pending clinical documentation
- Waiting for an order or medical-necessity review
- In a coding queue
- Awaiting a query response
- Held for late or missing charges
- In claim edits
- Awaiting payer follow-up
- Pending an appeal
- Waiting for a departmental escalation
- Assigned to an action plan that has not been completed


Time-at-handoff measures help leaders locate the actual bottleneck. They can reveal that a billing delay attributed to Patient Financial Services began several weeks earlier in documentation, coding, or authorization.


They can also show whether a workflow change solved the problem or simply moved the backlog to another department.


## Accountability should be specific without becoming punitive


The purpose of cross-functional reporting is not to create a list of “repeat offenders.” It is to distinguish among different types of problems so the organization can respond appropriately.


Recurring issues may result from:


- An unclear workflow
- Inadequate staffing or capacity
- Competing responsibilities
- Insufficient training
- Missing system access
- Poor system design
- An ineffective handoff
- A payer requirement
- A clinical-documentation delay
- A coding or charge-capture problem
- An individual performance concern


Those causes require different responses.


If the workflow is unclear, redesign it. If the employee lacks access, correct the access. If staffing is insufficient, address capacity and prioritization. If training is incomplete, provide education and validation. If the payer is creating the barrier, involve managed care or payer relations.


When expectations, workflow, training, access, and workload have all been addressed and the same responsibility continues to be missed, leadership may need to manage an individual performance issue. That is different from assuming every recurring error is an employee problem.


Senior-leadership reporting should therefore identify recurring error sources, repeated performance gaps, and areas where accounts consistently become stalled. That language keeps attention on the work while still preserving accountability.


## Include the patient’s experience in the review


The Revenue Cycle is not functioning well if internal KPIs improve while patients remain confused.


Leaders should examine whether patients are:


- Being asked for the same information repeatedly
- Receiving estimates early enough to make informed decisions
- Getting consistent explanations of their responsibility
- Being contacted by multiple departments about the same issue
- Learning about financial assistance early enough to use it
- Receiving delayed or inaccurate bills
- Waiting for care because an authorization or documentation issue was not escalated
- Calling because the organization’s internal handoffs were incomplete


A connected Revenue Cycle should reduce repeated contacts, improve the clarity of financial conversations, identify assistance earlier, and give patients confidence that the organization understands their account.


## Three actions leaders can take now


### 1. Map the complete workflow and define ownership at every handoff


Follow the account from scheduling through final resolution. Define “financially cleared,” “ready to bill,” and “complete” at each stage. Require every unresolved account to have an owner, next action, due date, and escalation path.


### 2. Establish shared KPIs and a biweekly cross-functional review


Include Patient Access, clinical operations, utilization management, documentation, coding, charge capture, billing, follow-up, denials, and Patient Financial Services. Review both departmental performance and the time accounts spend waiting between departments.


### 3. Require corrective-action plans and monthly senior-leadership oversight


Recurring performance gaps should have a documented root cause, accountable owner, correction deadline, and success measure. Senior leaders should see which actions are complete, which are overdue, where barriers remain, and where additional authority or resources are required.


## One patient, one account, one Revenue Cycle


The strongest Revenue Cycle organizations do not allow departmental boundaries to become stopping points.


They understand that an eligibility issue affects billing, a documentation delay affects coding, a coding backlog affects claims, a claim delay affects cash, and an inaccurate bill affects the patient’s trust in the entire organization.


Every department must own its work, but it must also understand the work that comes before and after it.


That requires clear definitions, closed-loop handoffs, shared measures, timely feedback, practical escalation, and leadership accountability.


The principle is straightforward:


**One patient, one account, one Revenue Cycle—and no unresolved work without a clear owner.**
